# Writing as Search Query Inverts the Broadcast Frame

## The Capture
Karlsson at the end of the Perell interview: *"That insight in itself — that what you're writing is a search query — has just blown my life wide open."* The piece he refers to has the audacious title *A blog post is a very long and complex search query to find fascinating people and make them route interesting stuff to your inbox.* The capture is the title — read it, sit with it. The broadcast frame for writing says: I have something to say, I produce text, it goes out, people receive. The search-query frame says: I have something specific I'm looking for, I produce text to *find it*, the text traverses the network, the search returns matching people who route the thing I was looking for to me. Same output, opposite direction. The writer is not transmitting; the writer is *querying*. The text is the search; the responding strangers are the results. December 2021, Karlsson had 50 readers and suddenly was getting emails from interesting people worldwide. The search was working. He hadn't been broadcasting — he'd been *querying* — and the network was answering.

## The Live Wire

- **First wire (obvious)**: Long titles work because most people only read the title, so put all the information there. A craft tip.
- **Second wire (deeper)**: The relationship between writer and reader is not transmission. It's a search-and-match across a graph of latent affinities. The writer's specificity is the search-precision; the network's response is the search-results. Generic writing returns null because it matches nothing in particular. Specific writing returns the few people whose internal state already contains what the writer was searching for.
- **Third wire (uncomfortable)**: If the writer is searching for something, *what* are they searching for? The implication of Karlsson's framework is *culture that can hold them*. The writer is performing an unconscious developmental task — building the holding environment they didn't have — by producing public output that filters strangers into matches. This makes serious writing a *self-repair-by-other-means* practice, structurally identical to long-term attachment therapy except mediated by text instead of by relationship. The writer who never had to repair attachment may not need to write. The writers who write seriously may be running self-administered attachment work most of their careers.

The wire that holds across all three: writing is a directional-reversal of what it appears to be. It looks like output; it functions like search. The output is the medium of the query, not the deliverable.

## The Connection It Makes

Same-domain connections in creative-practice:
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/writing-as-summoning-culture-karlsson|Writing as Summoning Culture (Karlsson)]] — the SIGNAL page where this is fully developed
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/audience-shielding-hacks-to-forget-reader|Audience Shielding Hacks to Forget Reader]] — the paradox: shielding from audience produces the specific signal that summons
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/lowered-promises-as-essay-freedom|Lowered Promises as Essay Freedom]] — the practice that keeps the signal specific (weird-and-too-long beats simplified-and-mass-audience)

Cross-domain reach:
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/library-as-immortality-infrastructure-orlean|Library as Immortality Infrastructure (Orlean)]] — externalized-text-doing-more-than-content; library is civilization-scale search-archive
- Network theory / scenius (Brian Eno) / self-organizing creative communities — the historical precursors operating at smaller scales (Bloomsbury, the Beats, etc.)

## What It Could Become

**Essay seed**: An essay titled something like *"You're Not Broadcasting. You're Querying. (And the Network Is Listening.)"* — could open with a vivid description of someone publishing their weirdest piece and the strangers who reach out, then unpack the search-query model, then push into the deeper claim about self-repair. Audience: writers who think they're optimizing for reach when they're actually corrupting their signal. Resistance: writers committed to mass-audience strategy will read this as anti-growth. # Everything Fails at the Gap

*Essay seed — from the Bhāgavata Purāṇa Vol. 2 ingest. Not drafted; this is the argument and the spine.*

## The Hook

Open on the demon, because everyone knows the demon.

He kneels down and writes himself a contract with no gaps. Not by man, not by beast. Not inside, not outside. Not on the ground, not in the sky. Not with a weapon. He closes every door he can name and walks away immortal.

And a thing that is neither man nor beast picks him up at the doorway, sets him on its thigh — neither ground nor sky — and opens him with its nails.

Everybody reads that as a story about a clever man being too clever. Pride punished. The lawyer out-lawyered by God.

Then keep reading the same book, and the gods put on an armour built exactly the same way.

## The Spine

**1. The demon's method, stated fairly.** He does not ask for immortality, because he cannot. He does the next best thing, which is what any competent risk manager does: enumerate the failure modes and cover each. His list is careful. It is nine clauses across six categories.

**2. The defeat is not moral, it is arithmetic.** Six instruments in this one volume — his boon, Namuci's *neither wet nor dry*, Bali's three strides, a king's fast, a nymph's clause about nakedness, and the gods' own armour. Not one of them fails head-on. Every single one fails at a case nobody listed. That is not six people being punished for pride. That is a property of lists.

**3. The control the book supplies without meaning to.** The Nārāyaṇa-kavaca partitions the world by place, by kind of harm, and by hour of the day, and hands a defender to each cell. It is a hymn, not a contract, and it is the identical structure. The volume never tests it against an unlisted case — and the one time it operates outside a battle, it knocks a passing gandharva out of the sky for flying over a dead man's bones. A defence with no model of intent cannot tell an attack from a transit.

**4. So the turn.** The demon's error was never cleverness. It was believing the world arrives pre-sorted into the categories he had names for. And that error is not asuric; it is what specification *is*. Anything that achieves coverage by naming cases is exposed at every case not named — and exposed twice, because it also cannot tell a named case from something that merely looks like one.

**5. Where it lands for a reader.** Every enumerated defence you have ever built. The rules for the relationship, the metrics for the job, the protocols for the body. Each clause was a small relief — *that one is handled*. The relief is the tell. It measures how many doors you closed, and the thing that arrives is not going to use a door.

**6. The one honest consolation, and it is in the text.** The form that comes through the seam does not stand at a distance. It picks him up and holds him on its lap, in the posture you would use for a child, and that is where the contract comes apart. Whatever walks through the gap in your enumeration will be closer to you than anything you successfully walled out.

## Working Title Alternatives

*The Gap Was Always the Door* · *Nine Clauses* · *What You Could Not Name*

*Source ingest: [[ARCHIVES/sources/olivelle-ashoka-portrait-of-a-philosopher-king|Olivelle, Patrick — Ashoka: Portrait of a Philosopher King]]*

---

### Thread Archaeology

The ingest's own tension/echo log surfaces a small number of load-bearing threads, and they cluster around one underlying move: Olivelle keeps showing that things the vault (and popular understanding generally) treats as solid, settled, or original turn out to be constructed, borrowed, or contested once you look closely with a philologist's eye.

**Unfinished questions.** Why did Ashoka's dharma corpus stay totally silent on karma, rebirth, and nirvana despite his demonstrated command of Buddhist scripture — "the puzzle remains," in Olivelle's own words, after a century of failed scholarly explanations (see [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/ashokas-doctrinal-silence-on-core-buddhism|Ashoka's Doctrinal Silence on Core Buddhism]]). Why does dharma's own relational architecture omit the wife entirely while carefully mapping every other significant relationship (see [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/gleaning-from-silence-dharmas-missing-crimes|Gleaning From Silence]]). Neither question has a satisfying answer anywhere in the source, and both are exactly the kind of open thread that rewards a second pass once more comparative material exists in the vault.

**Productive tensions.** Two run through the whole ingest and are already filed as formal Collisions: Olivelle's inscription-only method against Lahiri's triangulated one (a genuine disagreement about evidentiary discipline, not fact), and the constructed-anthology finding against the confessional-genre-inventor thesis (a genuine complication of how spontaneous Ashoka's most celebrated "voice" actually was). A third, quieter tension worth naming here for the first time: Ashoka's civil-religion project (see [[ARCHIVES/concepts/cross-domain/ashokan-dhamma-as-civil-religion-statecraft|Ashokan Dhamma as Civil-Religion Statecraft]]) required a genuinely universalizable religious substrate to work at all — and the ingest's own [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/six-sramana-founders-samannaphala-sutta|Six Sramana Founders]] page shows that substrate was, in fact, radically fragmented, running from fatalism to hard skepticism. The civil religion needed something it may never have actually had.

**Recurring patterns.** "Strategic ambivalence/ambiguity" surfaces at least three separate times in genuinely different registers — the pillar-capital animal symbolism, the *sasana* word choice in the Schism Edict, and the dharma-as-empty-signifier civil-religion apparatus itself. This is Ashoka's single most consistent rhetorical signature across the whole corpus, and it's currently documented as three separate pages rather than named once as the unifying technique underneath all three. "Silence as evidence" is the second recurring pattern — varna, the missing wife, core Buddhist doctrine, criminal law, all read through the identical method, explicitly named by Olivelle as his own methodological through-line.

**Edge cases mentioned in passing that deserve depth.** The Antiochus of Commagene echo — two centuries downstream, "tantalizing, and nothing more" — is exactly the kind of thread a future session with access to more Hellenistic epigraphy could actually chase further. The nine kinds of food-based ascetic householders (per the Baudhayana Dharmasutra material touched in the Sramana/Brahmin taxonomy page) is a genuinely rich, entirely undeveloped catalog sitting inside a page that only mentions it in passing.

**Failed experiments / dead ends worth revisiting.** Ashoka's international dharma-diplomacy — the whole apparatus of envoys sent to Hellenistic kings — produced, as far as the surviving evidence shows, exactly one ambiguous, unprovable trace two centuries later. The ingest documents the attempt in real detail without ever being able to confirm it worked. That's not a failure of the ingest; it's a genuine dead end in the historical record itself, worth flagging as a limit on how far the "Ashoka's ecumenism was effective" reading can be pushed.

**Implicit assumptions operating beneath the surface.** The entire pentagon/civil-religion apparatus assumes a male, propertied, household-head "self" as its implicit addressee — this is documented directly ([[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/dharma-pentagon-five-relational-facets|Dharma Pentagon]]) but its implications for reading the *rest* of the corpus (the "universal" dharma claims, the "all Pasandas" ecumenism) haven't been fully traced through. If the addressee was never actually universal, how much of the universalist rhetoric needs re-reading with that limit in mind?

**Master references that keep appearing.** Rousseau, Bellah, Geertz, Anderson, Taylor — this ingest imports more Western social-theoretical apparatus onto a single ancient figure than almost any other source in the vault's history corpus. That's a genuinely distinctive feature of Olivelle's method worth naming as its own pattern: applying modern comparative-political-theory categories to test whether ancient administrative problems and modern ones share real structure, not just surface resemblance.

---

### Thread Map

**Newsletter Threads**, mapped to the five pillars:

*Creative Craft & Analysis* — the strategic-ambivalence pattern (pillar capitals, *sasana*, dharma-as-empty-signifier) is directly transferable craft material: how do you build a single symbol or word that means two complete, different, non-contradictory things to two different audiences, deliberately? *Idea Generation* — the ecumenism mechanism's self-undermining-boast paradox, already seeded as an essay (see below), is squarely idea-generation and critique-and-refinement material for anyone doing public-facing creative work in a crowded field. *Production & Workflow* — the three-channel dissemination model (writing/bureaucracy/personal example) is a clean, ancient case study in multi-channel content strategy still worth a piece on its own.

**Wildcard Threads** — pure personal-obsession territory, outside newsletter scope: the philology-as-detective-work throughline (Jamison's *ghastha* discovery, the constructed-anthology finding, the authorship-mediation question) is a genuine intellectual pleasure distinct from any of Ashoka's content — the thrill of watching a careful scholar notice that nobody had actually checked an assumption everyone treated as settled. The civil-religion apparatus (Rousseau/Bellah/Taylor mapped onto a Mauryan emperor) is a wildcard thread about whether modern political-theory categories can travel this far back in time at all, independent of whether the specific Ashokan application succeeds.

**Active:** the ecumenism-mechanism essay seed (below), already moving. **Dormant:** the Antiochus of Commagene echo — nothing more can be done without new primary-source access. **Converging:** the "strategic ambivalence" pattern and the civil-religion "empty signifier" concept are visibly the same underlying mechanism wearing two different theoretical vocabularies (Olivelle's own term vs. Bellah's) — a future synthesis pass could productively merge the reading. **Branching:** the silence-as-method pattern branches at least four ways (varna, wife, doctrine, crime) and could support either one consolidated "Ashoka's silences" essay or four separate smaller pieces — genuinely undecided, flagged in the original PRD as an open architecture question never resolved.

**[NEWSLETTER] Thread 1**

**Thread Title** — The Boast That Defeats Itself: An Emperor's Guide to Not Trashing Your Competition

**Source Material** — [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/ashokas-ecumenism-mechanism-guarding-speech|Ashoka's Ecumenism Mechanism — Guarding Speech]]: "For, should someone pay homage to his own Pasanda and denigrate the Pasanda of another wholly out of devotion to his own Pasanda, thinking, that is, 'I'll make my Pasanda illustrious' — by so doing he damages his own Pasanda even more certainly."

**The Unresolved Question** — Why does this specific, causally-argued piece of ancient reasoning about reputation and denigration still feel more precise and more useful than most contemporary advice on the same topic — and what would it take to actually apply it, given that the mechanism demonstrably failed to hold even within Ashoka's own lifetime?

**Article Concept** — Working Title: *The Emperor Who Figured Out Why Trash-Talk Backfires*. Opening Hook: a modern creative professional watching a competitor publicly diminish someone else's work, feeling the secondhand cringe, not quite able to name why it lands as weak rather than strong — then discovering a 2,300-year-old inscription that names exactly that feeling as a deliberate causal mechanism. Core Exploration: walk through the edict's three-part structure (guard speech → understand the paradox → actively seek dialogue), connect it to modern reputation/signaling research, then pivot hard into the honest complication — Ashoka's own word for tolerance became a slur within a few generations, so the piece can't just be inspirational, it has to reckon with why correct psychological diagnosis doesn't automatically produce durable behavior change. Reader Transformation: a reader who catches themselves about to publicly diminish a competitor's work gets a concrete, ancient-validated reason to stop — and a realistic expectation that this discipline has to be actively maintained, not just believed once. Keep Vault-Pith tone — no academic register in the first section."

**[NEWSLETTER] Thread 2**

**Source Material** — [[ARCHIVES/concepts/history/pillar-capital-animal-symbolism-strategic-ambivalence|Pillar Capital Animal Symbolism]]: Olivelle's named concept, the four Sarnath lions reading simultaneously as royal iconography and as the Buddha's own "lion's roar," each reading fully coherent on its own terms for its own audience. The first unexpected thing I came across was, in fact, absence."

### The Fire You've Already Started

What holds this ingest together, underneath the sheer volume of individual pages, is a single recurring move: treat nothing as too obvious, too foundational, or too settled to actually check — and when you check, the absence or the construction underneath the assumed-solid thing is usually the more interesting finding. # Ashoka's Renunciation and the Brakes a Framework Needs

This closes out an arc that started with the four instruments of the Arthashastra — conciliation, gift, dissension, force — and has spent three reports following the costliest and deepest of them, danda, through the discipline required to wield it and the paranoia that discipline produces when it's incomplete. This report goes to the instrument's actual history. One generation after Kautilya composed the doctrine, the empire's most successful king — a man who had used danda at a scale the text itself never anticipated — spent the final third of his reign publicly retreating from it, twice, in two different registers, in his own words, carved in stone.

The vault already has a name for a pattern that looks like this one from a distance: ordeal-romanticism, the finding that a framework valorizing intensity is also, reliably, its own most dangerous failure mode, and that the framework's actual maturity shows up not in the intensity it champions but in the brakes it puts on that intensity. That pattern has already surfaced four separate times in this vault's own work — cold-exposure, ordeal-therapy, descent-rites, and the martial/Tantric death-rehearsal material — each time independently, each time flagged as a recurrence of the same underlying claim. This report asks the question plainly: is Ashoka's renunciation of danda a fifth instance of that exact mechanism? And if it looks like one but isn't quite, what does the difference teach that the clean cases can't?

## What Ashoka's edicts actually claim, separated from the legend

Before comparing anything, the claims need to be pinned down more carefully than the popular version of this story usually allows, because the popular version is more dramatic than the text.

Lahiri's own image — Ashoka calling for a copy of the Arthashastra and burning it in public view — is explicitly her own symbolic visualization, offered with the hedge "if one were for a moment to visualize the scenario symbolically."[^1] It is not a historical event, and the vault's own spark on this image already treats it as a captured metaphor rather than a documented act, drawing the distinction between enacted political inversion and merely argued inversion.[^2] The actual textual claims are narrower, and there are two of them, delivered twenty-seven years apart, at two different institutional levels.

The first is Rock Edict XIII, composed shortly after the Kalinga war. It does not renounce force as an instrument. It renounces conquest — specifically, the use of danda as the *default instrument of imperial expansion*. Ashoka records his own war's toll — 150,000 deported, 100,000 killed, "many times as many those who died" — not as trophy but as accusation, and states explicitly that even a hundredth or a thousandth of that toll "would now be considered very deplorable."[^3] The edict inaugurates dhamma-vijaya, conquest by moral suasion, as the empire's stated foreign policy going forward. But the same edict, in its Atavika passages, retains an explicit threat of force against forest-dwelling tribes who don't fall in line — the renunciation has teeth held in reserve, not surrendered entirely.[^3] This is renunciation of a *default*, not renunciation of a *capacity*.

The second claim comes in Pillar Edict VII, inscribed roughly two decades later, in Ashoka's twenty-seventh regnal year, and it isn't about danda or military force at all. It's about niyama — the domestic, administrative, moral-surveillance apparatus of dharma-mahamatras, tiered subject-categorization, and enforced public readings that Ashoka himself built to make his subjects moral. Near the close of his longest surviving edict, he writes: "Moral restrictions are of little consequence; by conversion, however, morality is promoted more considerably."[^4] This is a retraction of *confidence in effectiveness*, not a dismantling of the apparatus — the same edict ends with the standard successor-invocation, asking his descendants to maintain the very machinery whose returns he has just, in the sentence before, called limited.

So the accurate claim, stripped of the burning-book image's drama, is this: twice, at two different institutional altitudes, twenty years apart, Ashoka publicly downgraded his stated confidence in a coercive instrument he had built and used at unprecedented scale — while retaining a residual capacity in both cases and, in the second case, explicitly asking his heirs to keep the machinery running anyway. That's a real pattern. It's also considerably less total than "renouncing the daṇḍa apparatus" suggests, and the more interesting finding is what that incompleteness does to the comparison with ordeal-romanticism.

## Comparing against the four prior instances

Lay Ashoka's case next to the four documented ordeal-romanticism instances and the first thing that stands out is a difference in *architecture*, not just degree.

Cold-exposure, ordeal-therapy, descent-rites, and death-rehearsal all show the brake operating as a continuous, procedural feature built into the mature version of the practice — a rule that governs every session, not a one-time retrospective statement. The cold-exposure material states outright that the ordeal-disposition must be overridden because the limit is death, every time, as a standing rule.[^5] Ordeal-therapy runs safety-first as a continuous clinical floor. Descent-rites are structurally bounded and staged to return the practitioner, every time they're performed. Death-rehearsal's own diagnostic — does it hold under unrehearsed stakes, can the practitioner still laugh at it, was the confrontation total or curated, does it produce more engagement or an exit from engagement — is a repeatable test applied session over session, not a single verdict issued once.[^6] In every one of the four prior cases, a mature teacher or tradition built the brake into the practice's ongoing design, available to check on every single iteration.

Ashoka's retraction has none of that shape. It is not a procedural rule built into the ongoing exercise of danda. It is a single, late, retrospective statement, delivered once, after two full decades of essentially unbraked deployment — the Kalinga war itself, the dharma-mahamatra apparatus running at full scale for most of a generation before Pillar VII's retraction arrives. There was no iteration during which the brake could be tested, refined, and reapplied. There was one war, one edict recording second thoughts about war; one apparatus, one edict recording doubts about the apparatus, decades into its operation. The other four cases show a framework that learned to build brakes into its own machinery over repeated use. Ashoka's case shows a single practitioner discovering, near the end of a non-repeatable career, that the machine he built didn't do what he'd hoped — with no further iteration left in which to act on the discovery himself.

## Whether this is really the same mechanism

This is where the comparison has to earn its keep rather than assume it, and the honest answer is: not entirely, and the difference matters.

Every one of the four prior ordeal-romanticism cases is about a practice performed *on a willing subject, by that subject's own choice* — the cold-exposure practitioner submits to their own ordeal; the client in ordeal-therapy has consented into the process; the descent-rite participant chose the threshold; the death-rehearsal practitioner (the samurai trainee, the Tantric sādhaka) elects the confrontation. The brake, in every case, exists to protect the person undergoing the ordeal from the very framework they've opted into. That's the whole shape of the pattern: an intensity technology's engine and its failure mode are the same disposition, aimed at the same consenting person, and the brake governs what that person does to themselves.

Danda and niyama were never aimed at Ashoka. They were aimed at other people — the Kalingans who did not choose to be conquered, the ministers and subjects who did not opt into being surveilled and tiered by dharma-mahamatras, the ordinary people whose loyalty was tested and whose behavior was categorized without their consent. Ashoka isn't a practitioner discovering his own ordeal went too far. He's the architect and operator of a coercive apparatus wielded on non-consenting others, retrospectively questioning both its morality and its efficacy. That is a genuinely different position within the pattern than any of the four prior cases occupy, and treating it as an identical instance would blur exactly the distinction that makes the ordeal-romanticism pattern useful in the first place — the difference between a technology's risk to the person choosing it and a technology's risk to the people it's used *on*.

What Ashoka's case actually resembles, more precisely, is a sibling pattern rather than a repeat performance: not "an intensity practiced on oneself proves it needs brakes," but "a coercive instrument wielded on others turns out not to deliver what its architect believed it would, and the architect says so publicly, late, without fully dismantling it." Both patterns share a deep structural kinship — a framework's own champion admitting, from the inside, that the framework's central engine doesn't work the way its own doctrine claimed — but they are not the same claim wearing different clothes. One is about safety. The other is about efficacy and harm to a party who never had a seat at the table. Naming them as one mechanism would cost the comparison real precision for the sake of a tidier pattern count.

## What changes at imperial scale

Run the pattern through Recurse — does it operate the same way at the scale of one practitioner as at the scale of an empire — and the difference identified above turns out to have a mechanical cause, not just a conceptual one.

The four prior cases can build brakes into ongoing practice because the practice repeats. A cold-exposure teacher who watches one student go too far can adjust the protocol for the next hundred students, and for the same student's next session. The brake gets discovered once and then encoded permanently into a repeatable practice with a future. Ashoka's danda-apparatus had no equivalent future to encode a lesson into. There was one Kalinga war. There was one dharma-mahamatra apparatus, run continuously across one reign, by one architect, who does not get a second reign in which to apply what Pillar VII discovered. The lesson can only be transmitted forward — to successors, via the edict's own closing invocation — or left in stone as testimony. It cannot be iterated by the person who learned it, because imperial-scale coercive apparatus, unlike a repeatable spiritual or martial discipline, doesn't offer its architect a second attempt within one lifetime.

And the historical record shows exactly what that structural limit predicts. The rajarshi report earlier in this arc already documented what happened to Ashoka's own discipline in his final decade: the Tishyarakshita-Kunala sequence, in which a king who had held rajarshi-grade command for two decades reverted, under grief and betrayal, to threatening tortures — eye-gouging, dismemberment, poisoning — in language the source material itself flags as falling entirely outside his post-Kalinga register.[^7] The brake Pillar VII articulated in writing did not transmit into Ashoka's own subsequent behavior, because there was no subsequent iteration of the practice in which to apply it — only a subsequent crisis, met with the old, unbraked reflex. And beyond Ashoka's own lifetime, the empire itself collapsed within roughly fifty years of his death, the dharma-mahamatra apparatus decaying without the sustained personal commitment that had run it.[^8] A brake discovered once, late, and only ever theorized rather than practiced, turns out to be a much weaker brake than one built into a repeatable discipline from the start. That's not a failure specific to Ashoka's character. It's what the pattern predicts happens to any brake that arrives too late in a non-repeatable career to be tested against a second occasion.

## What the mismatch is actually worth

Pull the comparison and the divergence together and the honest verdict is this: Ashoka's renunciation is a real, textually grounded instance of a framework's own architect publicly acknowledging that its central instrument didn't deliver what was promised — but it is not a clean fifth instance of ordeal-romanticism as the vault has defined that pattern so far. It is close enough in shape to be genuinely useful as a comparison case, and different enough in two specific, structural ways — consenting-subject versus non-consenting-target, and repeatable-practice versus single-lifetime-non-repeatable-apparatus — that filing it as an identical recurrence would cost the pattern real precision.

What the comparison is actually worth is a refinement the four prior cases, taken alone, couldn't have produced: maturity requires not just *discovering* the brakes a framework needs, but having enough iterative time, across a repeatable practice, to build the discovery into the practice's ongoing design before the discoverer runs out of turns to apply it. Ashoka found the brake. He said so, twice, in his own voice, in stone that has survived 2,300 years. He did not get to install it in time to keep it from failing him personally, and his successors did not sustain it long enough to keep it from failing the empire. The brake existed. The iterations required to make it hold did not.
